name: Soga
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Nabirye, Minah 2016. A corpus-based grammar of Lusoga (PhD, Ghent Univ., 498pp) — likely covers prosody; fulltext not reachable (biblio.ugent.be errored). Wikipedia says only 'It is tonal.'

new_statements.quote: Prosody. Preliminary research indicates that Lusoga has a reversive tone system. Bantu languages whose tone system falls in this category have inverted the tones of Proto-Bantu reconstructed forms, i.e. H is realised as L and vice versa (Marlo 2013). Lusoga has four tones: H, L, HL and LH. Some of the tones create lexical contrast, as illustrated in the examples below.
new_statements.citation: Nabirye, Minah, Gilles-Maurice de Schryver & Jo Verhoeven. 2016. Lusoga (Lutenga). Illustrations of the IPA. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 46(2): 219-228. doi:10.1017/S0025100315000249
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lusoga is a lexical tone language (JIPA: four surface tones H, L, HL, LH; Hyman 2016: underlying privative /L/ vs. toneless, with H-tone plateauing/anticipation and a phrase-final H% boundary tone). No accessible source makes any statement about word stress, either a placement rule or an explicit 'no stress'; the JIPA Illustration's suprasegmental section is entirely about tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone-related: Hyman 2017 notes citation-form final vowel shortening (nouns never end in a long vowel) and predictable vowel length before NC; Hyman, Inkelas & Jenga 2016 describe penultimate prefixal V-lengthening only for Lulamogi, not Lusoga.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone plus post-lexical tone rules that Hyman 2017 shows apply across words regardless of syntactic constituency. JIPA data: Buwaabe (Bugweri county, Iganga district), one 40-year-old speaker, citation forms; Hyman's data: Lutenga speaker from Wairaka (Jinja district).
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted sources describe Lutenga, the standard Lusoga variety (Glottolog soga1242 covers it; no separate glottocode for Lutenga). JIPA 2016 speaker from Buwaabe, Bugweri county, Iganga district; Hyman's speaker from Wairaka, Jinja district; Yukawa's informant from Iganga. Lulamogi, sometimes lumped under 'Lusoga', is treated by Hyman as dialectal with Lugwere (gwer1238) and its penultimate-lengthening facts should not be attributed to Lusoga.

sources.quote: Prosody. Preliminary research indicates that Lusoga has a reversive tone system. Bantu languages whose tone system falls in this category have inverted the tones of Proto-Bantu reconstructed forms, i.e. H is realised as L and vice versa (Marlo 2013). sources.note: The suprasegmental section ('Prosody', p. 226) is tone only: reversive tone system, four tones H, L, HL, LH, some lexically contrastive. The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the article. Variety: Buwaabe, Bugweri county, Iganga district, one 40-year-old speaker. PDF was served by Cambridge Core without login; the landing page does not label it OA (Ghent biblio lists the file as restricted).
Says only 'It is tonal.'; cites the JIPA illustration for phonology.

sources.citation: Nabirye, Minah. 2023. Language documentation for Lusoga (Bantu, JE16). Abstract, Tokyo African Linguistics Knot, TUFS, 2 March 2023.
sources.note: One-page abstract listing Nabirye's publications; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2017. Bantu tone overview. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 13.
sources.note: Cites Soga [JE16] for H-tone shift onto the preceding TBU, a final H% boundary tone, and HL falling on a long penult (e-seente 'money'); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2017. In search of prosodic domains in Lusoga. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 13. doi:10.5070/P7131040753
sources.note: Post-lexical tone rules (H tone plateauing/anticipation) apply across the board without syntactic domains. 'Word stress' appears only in a comparison with Bella Coola (46b); nothing about Lusoga stress. Mentions penultimate lengthening only as a general Bantu expectation.

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2017. Lusoga noun phrase tonology. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 13. doi:10.5070/P7131040747
sources.note: Noun and NP tone; notes final vowel shortening (citation forms never have a long final vowel) and predictable length before NC. No statement on stress.

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2016. The autosegmental approach to tone in Lusoga. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 12: 1-22. doi:10.5070/P7121040726 (reprinted 2018 in Shaping Phonology, Univ. of Chicago Press)
sources.note: Analyses Lusoga (Lutenga; speaker Fr. Fred Jenga, Wairaka) as a privative /L/ vs. O tone system; infinitive tone patterns, nouns, reduplication. No mention of stress or accent placement (the only 'accentual' remark is a general Bantu-typology aside, p. 1).

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M., Sharon Inkelas & Fred Jenga. 2016. Multiple exponence in the Lusoga verb stem. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 12: 125-141. doi:10.5070/P7121040725 (also in Bowern, Horn & Zanuttini (eds) 2017, On looking into words, Language Science Press, 171-188)
sources.note: fn. 2 (p. 130): 'Lusoga has a /L/ vs. O tone system (Hyman 2016)'. pp. 137-138 describe penultimate prefixal V-lengthening and pre-penultimate shortening for Lulamogi (not Lusoga). No stress statement.

sources.citation: de Schryver, Gilles-Maurice & Minah Nabirye. 2010. A quantitative analysis of the morphology, morphophonology and semantic import of the Lusoga noun. Africana Linguistica 16: 97-153.
sources.note: Corpus-based noun morphology; no tone or stress description. Bibliography cites Yukawa 2000 and Van der Wal 2004.

sources.citation: Yukawa, Yasutoshi. 2000. Soga-go doushi akusento shiron [A tentative tonal analysis of Soga verbs]. Journal of Asian and African Studies (ILCAA, Tokyo) 60: 249-290. doi:10.15026/21873
sources.note: Scan without text layer (no Japanese tessdata on our machine); pp. 249-251 rendered to ocr_yukawa/ and read as images. p. 249 (English summary): 'The verbs in this language are tonally divided into two groups.' p. 250: acute over a vowel (or preconsonantal nasal) marks 'high', unmarked = 'low'; a word-final 'high' is often pronounced with a falling contour when nothing follows. 'Akusento' here means tone; no stress statement. Informant born 1977 in Iganga.
